questions.title: What exactly is the rescaling formula for RoPE in LongRoPE (notation confusion around \(\lambda\), \(\hat{\lambda}\), and \(\beta\))?
questions.question_body:
I'm confused by the unified RoPE expression used in the paper. The standard RoPE for position \(n\) uses angles \([\cos(n\theta_0), \sin(n\theta_0), \ldots]\) with \(\theta_i = \theta^{-2i/d}\) and \(\beta = \theta^{2/d}\), so the per-dimension angle can be written as \(\frac{n}{\beta^i}\).

For interpolation, the paper writes something like \(\cos\big(\frac{n}{\lambda(\beta)^i}\big)\) and later defines per-dimension factors \(\lambda_i\) and also uses \(\hat{\lambda}_i = 1/\lambda_i\), and a position gating function \(\mathbb{I}(\hat{\lambda}_i, \hat{n})\). Can someone clarify the exact angle used per dimension/head/layer? Is it:
- \(\cos\big(\frac{n}{\lambda_i\,\beta^i}\big)\) for \(n \ge \hat{n}\) and \(\cos\big(\frac{n}{\beta^i}\big)\) for \(n < \hat{n}\), or
- \(\cos\big(\mathbb{I}(\hat{\lambda}_i,\hat{n})\cdot \frac{n}{\beta^i}\big)\) with \(\mathbb{I}\) either 1 or \(1/\lambda_i\)?
Also, is \(\lambda\) ever a function of \(\beta\), or is it always dimension-specific constants \(\{\lambda_i\}\)?

questions.title: Why impose a monotonic non-decreasing constraint \(\lambda_i \le \lambda_{i+1}\) across RoPE dimensions?
questions.question_body: The search enforces \(\lambda_i \le \lambda_{i+1}\) over the half-dimensions (i.e., lower-indexed, higher-frequency dimensions receive less interpolation). I understand the NTK-inspired intuition, but is there a theoretical reason this monotonicity should always hold for optimal interpolation? Could an optimal solution violate monotonicity due to model- or layer-specific idiosyncrasies? Do you have ablations showing performance when the constraint is removed or relaxed?

questions.title: How is discontinuity at the threshold \(\hat{n}\) avoided when the first \(\hat{n}\) tokens are not interpolated?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes preserving the first \(\hat{n}\) positions, i.e., for \(n<\hat{n}\), use the original angles \(\frac{n}{\beta^i}\), and for \(n\ge\hat{n}\), use rescaled angles \(\frac{n}{\lambda_i\,\beta^i}\). Doesn't this create a potential phase discontinuity around \(n=\hat{n}\) for each dimension? Is there any adjustment (e.g., an additive phase shift) to ensure continuity at \(\hat{n}\), or is the model robust to this jump? If no continuity correction is used, do you observe artifacts in attention around the boundary?

questions.title: Are the per-dimension scale factors \(\{\lambda_i\}\) shared across layers and heads, or learned separately?
questions.question_body: RoPE is typically applied per head with head dimension \(d_{\text{head}}\), yielding \(d_{\text{head}}/2\) angles per head. When LongRoPE searches \(\{\lambda_i\}\), are these indices \(i\) defined within each head (so each head has its own \(\lambda_{i,\text{head}}\)), or globally shared across all heads and layers? If shared, how do you map \(i\) across heads when their positions in the concatenated embedding space differ? If per-head or per-layer specialization is not used, did you test whether allowing it would help?

questions.title: What does it mean that YaRN "doesn't reach the target context length" in non-fine-tuned settings?
questions.question_body: In the analysis, you state that YaRN underperforms on PG19 and "doesn't reach the target context window length" for non-fine-tuned LLMs (e.g., perplexity spikes after 7k in an 8k context). What is the precise criterion for "reaching" the target length? Is it defined by a perplexity threshold, stability of loss, or something else? Could you formalize this notion so different methods can be compared consistently?

questions.title: Why allow \(\lambda_i\) up to \(1.25\,s\)? How does this ensure coverage of positions up to \(L'\)?
questions.question_body: The search space for each \(\lambda_i\) is \([1.0,\,1.25\,s]\) with step 0.01, where \(s=L'/L\) is the target extension ratio. Intuitively, PI uses \(\lambda=s\) to map \([0, L')\) back into \([0,L)\). If \(\lambda_i > s\), then \(n=L'\) maps to \(L'/\lambda_i < L\), i.e., even stronger compression. What is the benefit of permitting \(\lambda_i > s\)? Conversely, if some \(\lambda_i < s\), that dimension effectively extrapolates beyond the original range—how do you ensure that collectively the representation remains faithful for positions up to \(L'\)?

questions.title: How robust is the evolutionary search to overfitting on the small validation subsets used for perplexity?
questions.question_body: For search, you evaluate perplexity on 5 PG19 samples (within 256k) or 3 Books3 samples (beyond 512k). Given the very large search space and many evaluations, how do you prevent overfitting the rescale factors to these specific texts? Did you validate that the chosen \(\{\lambda_i\}, \hat{n}\) generalize across domains and random seeds? Any evidence like train-vs-test perplexity gaps or re-running search on different subsets?

questions.title: Why does keeping the first \(\hat{n}\) tokens un-interpolated help, and how should \(\hat{n}\) scale with \(L'\)?
questions.question_body: The paper reports that preserving the first \(\hat{n}\) tokens without interpolation improves perplexity and that the optimal \(\hat{n}\) depends on the target length. Can you provide intuition or a simple model for how attention distributions make early tokens especially sensitive to interpolation? Also, is there a principled way to choose \(\hat{n}\) as a function of \(L'\) (e.g., proportional to \(\log L'\), a fixed count, or learned via search)?

questions.title: How do you compute perplexity for very long contexts during search without prohibitive cost?
questions.question_body:
Evaluating perplexity at lengths like 256k or higher can be extremely expensive if done naively due to quadratic attention in the prefill. What practical steps did you take during search to keep evaluation tractable? For example:
- Do you use a sliding window and cache K/V across windows?
- Any approximations, chunked attention, or reduced precision?
- Typical wall-clock time and GPU memory for one fitness evaluation at 256k and at 2M tokens?

questions.title: Does LongRoPE adjust the RoPE base \(\theta\) (e.g., 10000), and could base changes be equivalent to certain \(\lambda_i\) schedules?
questions.question_body: Standard RoPE uses \(\theta=10000\), which induces \(\beta=\theta^{2/d}\) and angles \(\frac{n}{\beta^i}\). LongRoPE rescales via \(\{\lambda_i\}\). If one instead changed \(\theta\) (globally or per-layer/head), would this be functionally equivalent to a particular pattern of \(\{\lambda_i\}\) for some ranges of \(n\)? Did you consider searching over base \(\theta\) or combining base changes with per-dimension \(\lambda_i\) for additional flexibility?

questions.title: How are different \(\{\lambda_i\}\) sets selected at inference time for short vs long sequences?
questions.question_body: For short-context recovery, you search separate rescale factors for 4k/8k and dynamically switch if the sequence length is less than 8k. Implementation-wise, does the model carry multiple RoPE configurations and pick one based on the current sequence length? If a sequence grows from 6k to 10k during generation, do you switch RoPE mid-generation? If so, how do you avoid distribution shift or discontinuities when the factors change?

questions.title: What exactly are the "catastrophic values" introduced by new positions, and how does interpolation prevent them?
questions.question_body: The introduction mentions that untrained new position indices introduce many catastrophic values, making fine-tuning hard to converge. Can you spell out what these catastrophic values are at the level of attention logits or hidden states? For example, do large angles cause destructive interference in QK dot products or numerical overflow/underflow in \(\sin/\cos\) at big \(n\)? How does your non-uniform interpolation specifically mitigate these failure modes?

questions.title: How does LongRoPE mitigate attention dispersion at extreme lengths without changing the attention mechanism?
questions.question_body: One challenge is that attention becomes dispersed as \(L'\) grows, hurting short-context performance. LongRoPE claims to preserve important positional information via non-uniform interpolation. Can you provide intuition or quantitative evidence (e.g., attention heatmaps or entropy) that shows reduced dispersion compared to PI/NTK/YaRN? Since you do not modify masks or sparsity, how exactly does adjusting \(\{\lambda_i\}\) counteract dispersion?

questions.title: Does the two-stage progressive strategy amount to composing two scalings, or is the second search done from scratch?
questions.question_body: The method fine-tunes at 128k→256k with searched factors, then performs a second search on the 256k model to reach 2048k without further fine-tuning. Is the second stage initializing from the first stage's \(\{\lambda_i\}, \hat{n}\) and then refining, or does it search from scratch over the full space again? Mathematically, if the first stage applies \(\lambda_i^{(1)}\) and the second stage \(\lambda_i^{(2)}\), is the effective mapping equivalent to a single scaling by \(\lambda_i^{(1)}\,\lambda_i^{(2)}\), or do you replace the first set entirely?

questions.title: Why does LongRoPE achieve about \(8\times\) extension without fine-tuning—what breaks beyond that?
questions.question_body: You report that the non-fine-tuned extension reliably works up to roughly \(8\times\) while PI/NTK/YaRN often break earlier. Is there a conceptual reason why \(\sim8\times\) is a practical limit (e.g., unavoidable aliasing across dimensions, loss of phase information, or compounding approximation error)? What symptoms appear first when pushing to, say, \(16\times\) without finetuning?

questions.title: What is the definition of "information entropy" of positional embeddings used to justify non-uniformity?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions "complex non-uniform information entropy" in the Transformer regarding positional embeddings. How is this entropy quantified? Is it the entropy of attention distributions conditioned on positions, the spectrum of positional encoding across layers, or something else? Could you share the exact metric and empirical plots that motivated the per-dimension and per-position non-uniform treatment?

questions.title: Why do Mistral fine-tuning runs use 16k training length while targeting 128k/256k windows?
questions.question_body: In the setup, for Mistral you follow YaRN and use 16k sequence length during fine-tuning while still calling the resulting models 128k/256k. How does this training length mismatch relate to the target context window? Is the idea that the searched RoPE provides the length generalization, with relatively short fine-tuning just anchoring the model? Any downsides observed (e.g., worse performance beyond 256k for Mistral compared to LLaMA2)?

questions.title: How do you ensure numerical stability of \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) at positions near 2M tokens?
questions.question_body: With angles like \(\frac{n}{\lambda_i\,\beta^i}\) and \(n\) up to \(2{,}048{,}000\), do you encounter numerical issues in float16/float32 evaluation of \(\sin\) and \(\cos\)? For instance, precision loss for large arguments can be severe. Do you reduce angles modulo \(2\pi\) explicitly, use higher precision for angle computation, or employ stable rotary implementations to avoid catastrophic cancellation?

questions.title: How is passkey retrieval at 2M tokens executed within memory constraints?
questions.question_body: For the passkey task up to 2,048k context, prefill attention is \(O(L'^2)\) compute and memory if done in one shot, which seems infeasible. Did you use chunked prefill, streaming with KV cache, or other engineering to run inference? Could you outline the exact inference procedure (batch size, precision, number of GPUs, peak memory) used to obtain the reported accuracy curves?

questions.title: Is there an invertibility or separation guarantee to avoid position aliasing after interpolation?
questions.question_body: For distinct positions \(n_1 \neq n_2\), after applying non-uniform interpolation, the rotated embeddings across all dimensions should remain sufficiently distinct to let attention discriminate them. Is there any condition on \(\{\lambda_i\}\) ensuring that the mapping \(n \mapsto [\cos(\cdot),\sin(\cdot)]\) remains injective (or at least collision-resistant) over \([0,L')\)? Could bad choices of \(\{\lambda_i\}\) lead to aliased positions that are indistinguishable to the model?

questions.title: How exactly is perplexity computed during search for samples longer than \(L'\)?
questions.question_body:
The optimization problem specifies inputs \(\mathbf{X}\) where each document length exceeds \(L'\). During fitness evaluation, do you:
- Take the first \(L'\) tokens and compute NLL on the next-token targets across that range?
- Use a sliding window of size \(L'\) and average losses across windows?
- Evaluate only on the tail to stress long-range dependencies?
Clarity on this evaluation protocol would help interpret the reported perplexities and search outcomes.
